page5_img_1.png.title: IDE screenshot showing Copilot multi-line TypeScript suggestion
page5_img_1.png.description: A dark‑themed editor (file tab sentiments.ts) displaying a TypeScript async function isPositive(text: string): Promise<boolean>. A multi-line Copilot suggestion is highlighted in blue and inserts a fetch call to 'http://text-processing.com/api/sentiment/' with options (method: "POST", body: `text=${text}`, headers including "Content-Type": "application/x-www-form-urlencoded"). The code continues with const json = await response.json(); return json.label === "pos"; and a Copilot badge is visible in the bottom-left, illustrating that the tool can produce context-aware, multi-line completions in the IDE. Other open tabs (write_sql.go, parse_expenses.py, addresses.rb) hint at multi-language use.

page9_img_table_1.png.title: Three-column summary of early Copilot user experiences
page9_img_table_1.png.description: A three-column table titled “THE GOOD / THE BAD / THE MIXED” that condenses early Copilot forum feedback into short, stacked entries (rows separated by dotted red lines). The Good column highlights perceived benefits such as reported productivity improvements, comparisons of Copilot to a human pair programmer, Copilot “removing the ceiling on creativity,” and suggestions users would have otherwise overlooked. The Bad column lists concrete concerns: Copilot getting stuck in loops of repeated suggestions, failing to write defensive checks (e.g., null-pointer checks), sometimes suggesting inappropriate text, and occasionally leaking PII in header files. The Mixed column captures ambiguous trade-offs users noted: less manual coding but more time spent reviewing suggestions, reduced reliance on Stack Overflow paired with less understanding of why code works, and limited API discoverability that doesn’t give enough information to choose the best solution.

page4_img_table_1.png.title: Three-study summary of Copilot research and key findings
page4_img_table_1.png.description: A three-column summary table that compares the paper’s three empirical studies: Study 1 (Forum analysis, Oct–Nov 2021) reviewed 279 GitHub Discussions posts to answer “What are people using Copilot for?” and found users spent less time on Stack Overflow but reported having less understanding of how or why suggested code works. Study 2 (Case study, Dec–Jan 2022) used a think‑aloud protocol with five expert Python developers to explore how first‑timers engage with Copilot and found participants accepted suggestions for efficiency while relinquishing a small amount of autonomy/control and visibly wrestling with that tradeoff in real time. Study 3 (Survey, Feb–Mar 2022) analyzed 2,047 survey responses to assess productivity, correlating 11 usage metrics with perceived productivity and reporting that acceptance rate showed the strongest positive relationship (acceptance rate had the highest positive correlation to aggregate perceived productivity; reported in the text as ρ ≈ 0.24, P < 0.0001). The table layout highlights each study’s question, approach (in red), and concise key finding (in red) beneath dotted separators.
